item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras remained absent from the Red Sox’ lineup Thursday night at Fenway Park, seven days after he got hit by a pitch and bruised his right hand.
Is it fair to say he will be ready for the start of the playoffs?
“I hope so,” manager Chad Tracy said before the team’s finale with the Guardians. “I hope so. But [the Red Sox] want to see how he gets through all this stuff and where he’s at. And my hope is — at least for now — that he swings and feels even better than he did the other day, and then we’ll go from there.”
The first baseman took batting practice in the indoor cage, as he did earlier in the week.
It would be “huge,” Tracy said, if he was ready in time to play at any point during the Cubs series. Otherwise, he may well roll into the AL Wild Card Series without having faced live pitching in nearly two weeks.
“But I also think you’re talking about a guy [who has] a pretty good idea of his swing,” Tracy said. “[With] Willson not being down that long, the most important thing is that he’s healthy. So if he’s healthy and feeling good about it, where we’re able to get him some at-bats, that’d be great. But we’re still going to be reactive to how he’s feeling.”
Weather watch
The Cubs-Red Sox series remains in flux.
They will attempt to play a doubleheader at Fenway Park on Friday, with 1 p.m. and 6 p.m. first pitches, before a potential nor’easter arrives.
Yet to be decided: where and when the teams play their regular-season finale. Although it is scheduled for 7:15 p.m. Saturday in Boston, it could be moved to another venue, such as Tampa Bay, if the weekend forecast remains horrendous.
If the game is moved, the clubs would leave Friday night and likely play at 3 p.m. Sunday, same as all of the other finales.
MLB and the teams intend to make a call by midday Friday about what to do about Game 162.
“In a nutshell, it doesn’t look good. That’s basically what I’ve heard,” Tracy said of the weather. “Seems like we should be able to get that [doubleheader] in even [if during] the second game there might be a little bit of drizzle or whatever. It doesn’t look bad, at least what I’m seeing, and then figure out what happens next.”
Crochet on the move
A wrinkle from the weather: Garrett Crochet (left shoulder injury) will head to Fort Myers, Fla., on Friday so that he can throw an inning of live batting practice on Saturday.
The Sox have a stash of Triple-A hitters, including infielders Romy Gonzalez and Franklin Arias, working out at Fenway South.
Rafaela OK
Ceddanne Rafaela turned out to be just fine after a scare Wednesday.
The Thursday MRI on his right hamstring came back “clean,” Tracy said, affirming Rafaela’s stance from the night prior that his exit after two innings was no big deal.
“The feel is that it was a cramp, probably actually precipitated by the diving catch an inning prior],” Tracy said. “He tends to dive, and he does have low back/hip stuff that throws him out of the line for a second, that’ll manifest itself in feeling [the hamstring].”
Rafaela was back in the lineup against the Guardians, batting sixth and playing center field. It was his second game back from a right quad strain.
Major honors from minors
The Red Sox announced their annual minor league award winners, a group headed by Arias, the offensive player of the year. He slashed .323/.400/.557 with 25 homers and 91 RBIs in 117 games with Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, emerging as one of the top prospects in all of the minors.
Lefthander Dylan Brown was named pitcher of the year. A 22-year-old starter, he had a 3.46 ERA and 143 strikeouts in 106⅔ innings with Low-A Salem and High-A Greenville.
Other honored were catcher Gerardo Rodriguez (defensive player of the year), outfielder Andrews Opata (baserunner of the year), outfielder Joskairo Ramirez (Latin program position player of the year), and righthander Emanuel Jimenez (Latin program pitcher of the year).
Mead update
Infielder Curtis Mead (left wrist fracture) plans to take another step forward Friday by taking batting practice off of a machine. He will head to Fort Myers with Crochet and potentially hit against him on Saturday, he said. He is not ruled out for the first round of the playoffs beginning Tuesday, but that deadline might be too soon … Tracy left Roman Anthony out of the lineup to give him a day off. The outfielder had started 22 consecutive games since returning from the IL, batting .242 with a .726 OPS … Eli White was back at Fenway for the first time since season-ending right foot surgery Tuesday. He said he is due for a three-month recovery. That timeline would allow the outfielder to get almost all the way back to full health before the expected lockout on Dec. 1, at which point teams will not be allowed to communicate with players … Infielder Anthony Seigler said he was diagnosed with a carpal boss, a bony lump on the back of his right hand/wrist — the same injury that plagued catcher Connor Wong last year. Wong wound up having surgery to get it removed. Seigler said he has not discussed that possibility with the Red Sox … DH/outfielder Masataka Yoshida (left hamstring strain) appeared on the field at Fenway, playing catch and doing light agility drills … Dustin Pedroia and his family, in town this week, were on the field about five hours before first pitch against Cleveland, chatting with Red Sox personnel. His three sons made sure to poke their head into the Green Monster.

item.content:encoded:
Barring an unforeseen collapse or miracle, the Boston Red Sox will be heading to New York for the Wild Card series for the second consecutive season. After scoring just six runs in their three-game series against the Yankees last year — including a shutout in the decisive Game 3 — it figures that the offense will be the primary topic of conversation prior to the 2026 iteration of this epic playoff rivalry.
That's especially true right now, since the Red Sox have apparently completely lost their ability to hit in clutch situations over the past month. For reference, in nine of their first 15 games of September, they went hitless or managed just one hit with runners in scoring position.
That has a lot of people wondering: Is it time to do something drastic to shake up the run-production unit? Hence, the idea of calling up speed demon Braiden Ward has started to gain some traction recently, since he's managed a whopping 61 steals in 109 games in Worcester this year.
The problem, of course, is that the Red Sox need someone who can deliver hits with runners in scoring position, rather than just someone who can get in scoring position. And if a call-up is in the cards, it's clear that Romy Gonzalez is most deserving. He and Ward are both part of a "stay ready" squad the Red Sox have sent to Fort Myers in the event of a playoff call-up.
Romy Gonzalez has earned another stint with Red Sox following torrid stretch in Worcester
Gonzalez didn't have the easiest time in Boston earlier this year, posting a 59 wRC+ over 19 games after being activated off the 60-day injured list. Since being sent down to Triple-A to work on his game in early August, however, he was a total menace at the plate in the final weeks of the WooSox season: he hit .355/.410/.538 with 11 extra-base hits in just 93 at-bats.
That's the kind of run-producing bat the big-league club needs at the moment. There is merit in giving Ward a bench role in the playoffs — his speed and defense would be huge assets late in games — but nothing he provides would be as valuable as having Gonzalez's career 131 wRC+ against southpaws available at a moment's notice.
Another consideration? Ward, who has never played in the majors, isn't currently on the 40-man roster and would need to be added ahead of a playoff series, displacing someone else. That would probably be as simple as stashing Curtis Mead on the 60-day IL, but it would also begin Ward's service time clock just ahead of the impending lockout.
With all due respect to Ward, the Red Sox already made their call on him at the trade deadline, when they acquired a player with a very similar profile in Eli White. His injury may have seemingly opened the door for a call-up, but with runs at a premium in October, the wisest course of action is to go with the bat-first player with extensive MLB action under his belt.

item.content:encoded:
Alongside the news that beloved interim skipper Chad Tracy will drop his interim tag, the Boston Red Sox got a slew of positive injury updates. Boston is just six games from the postseason and it needs all the reinforcements it can get.
One of the best, if not the best update is that Willson Contreras is swinging a bat following a scary hit by pitch against the Texas Rangers. Contreras on September 17 took a pitch on the side of his hand, immediately fell to the ground in pain and left the game without delay.
Contreras doesn't easily leave games after being plunked, which has happened 24 times this season. His immediate departure led fans to believe he could've been severely injured. Thankfully, that was not the case, as his imaging came back clean. He believed he fractured his hand because it was numb for a few minutes after the hit, but Contreras avoided the worst.
The Red Sox have not announced an estimated return date for Contreras, but any progress is a good sign. He's been Boston's best hitter all season and leads the team in home runs — the Sox can't afford to go to the postseason without him, especially with the New York Yankees' fearsome rotation ahead in the Wild Card series.
Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela near returns to Red Sox after both take batting practice on September 22
Ceddanne Rafaela also took batting practice on September 22. He hit off Garrett Crochet, who threw 16 pitches before Contreras' turn in the batter's box. The outfielder on September 19 told Alex Speier of The Boston Globe that he hopes to be active for the final homestand of the season, which has already started.
Like Contreras, Rafaela has been one of Boston's most consistent hitters all year. The Soxs offense has faltered without the two in the lineup. If his timeline holds, Rafaela should be back before the postseason so the Red Sox can take full advantage of his clutch timing in huge moments.
Rumors swirl about Curtis Mead's recovery following Garrett Crochet's BP session
There were also rumors that Curtis Mead was expected to hit off Crochet following Rafaela's practice, but there has been no confirmation that he actually swung a bat. The Red Sox acquired Mead from the Washington Nationals at the trade deadline to bring a righty power bat to their lineup, but he was plunked in his second Red Sox at-bat and the pitch fractured his wrist.
The most recent update on Mead from mid-September was that he was still feeling soreness in his wrist when he tried to swing. The soreness would need to subside for his hitting progression to start, and given the time of the season, many people assumed his year had reached its end. Given that he may not have hit against Crochet, it might still be.
Red Sox send Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo to Fort Myers to stay loose in case of postseason use
Alongside Crochet, the Red Sox have starters-turned-relievers Tanner Houck and Johan Oviedo nearing the end of their respective recoveries. Both pitchers made rehab assignments with the Triple-A Worcester Red Sox before their season ended and they've been sent to Fort Myers to stay loose just in case Boston needs them in the playoffs, according to Chris Cotillo of MassLive.
The Red Sox will have no shortage of pitching depth entering the playoffs, but whether they use any of their rehabbing pitchers is still yet to be seen. Well-rested arms would be helpful, but the team could be concerned about upsetting the chemistry of the preexisting bullpen, which has been one of the best in the sport all year.

item.content:encoded:
Garrett Crochet reached an important milestone in his road to recovery on Tuesday, facing live hitters on the mound at Fenway Park for the first time since his ill-fated comeback attempt in late May.
Throwing live batting practice against Ceddanne Rafaela, the Red Sox ace threw 16 pitches, one more than originally planned because he spiked a changeup into the dirt on what was supposed to be his final pitch. The left-hander said he was able to ramp up his intensity to a level he hadn’t reached yet, that his fastball was in the 94-96 mph range, and that following the session he got good feedback from Rafaela.
With that crucial box checked, could Crochet’s next time on the mound come in a game setting? Crochet said it’s too soon to say, but he’s cautiously optimistic about his ability to do so.
“You don’t know until you know I suppose. I would say the way that live just went that I could go get outs,” Crochet said. “It depends, obviously, what role they want me in, like I said it’s not really for me to say, I know myself and I know my body, and the biggest thing is that I felt good out there.”
Crochet has missed the majority of the season due to left shoulder inflammation, which landed him on the injured list in late April after only six starts. What was originally believed to be a short-term injury wound up sidelining Crochet for five months and counting, but after Tuesday’s session there remains a possibility Crochet could factor into the postseason equation for the Red Sox out of the bullpen.
That will be up to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy, Crochet was sure to emphasize.
“This team has had a great year, I think for me to take a spot on the roster then someone would have to lose one, and I would feel bad doing that because this team has pitched their (butts) off the whole season,” Crochet said. “Ultimately that’s going to be something that’s up to the front office and whenever they gauge that I’m ready then I’ll accept that, and in the meantime I’m just going to keep working my butt off.”
Tracy said he was encouraged by Crochet’s outing, noting that his velocity is climbing and the spin on his pitches looked sharp. The next step will be seeing how his body recovers in the upcoming days and mapping out a plan for the weekend.
“What that looks like now, I don’t know,” Tracy said. “I just know that whatever it is it’s going to be done with Garrett’s best interest in mind.”
Typically the next stage in a throwing progression after throwing live batting practice would be to start a rehab assignment, but given that the minor league season ended this past weekend, that isn’t an option for Crochet. Time also isn’t on the left-hander’s side, so if Crochet is going to pitch in a game before the playoffs, he would have to be activated at some point over the final homestand.
Tracy said those are all factors the club is considering, and while he believes Crochet would be up for the challenge of jumping right into a playoff series, they have to be realistic about where he’s at when it comes time to decide who will be on the playoff roster.
“Knowing the player, if he was healthy and we felt he could he’d probably be like ‘I’m not going to be afraid of that,'” Tracy said. “That being said, we have to consider it and just be very mindful of what are we potentially exposing him to and what can he give us, really? Understanding you don’t want to leave yourself short, so for me it’s been step by step, the next step would be sometime this weekend, let’s see what that entails, and we’ll go from there.”
Rafaela, Contreras getting close
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) remain sidelined with their respective injuries, but Tracy said both are getting close to a return.
“(Rafaela) is doing much better, we’re getting close there, and Willson’s also doing much better, he was able to swing pretty aggressively in the cage again today,” Tracy said, adding that Rafaela was scheduled to run and Contreras was set to take batting practice on the field. “(We’ll) let them get through their whole day, see where they’re at and assess, but I think we’re getting pretty close with both of them.”
Staying ready
With the minor league season finished the Red Sox have sent a contingent of players who may potentially factor into the club’s plans the rest of the way to Fort Myers so they can stay ready in the event they’re needed.
Tracy did not have the full list of players available when asked Tuesday, but some of those headed to Fort Myers include pitchers Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Jedixson Paez, Tyler Samaniego and Wyatt Olds, infielders Romy Gonzalez, Franklin Arias and Tsung-Che Cheng, and outfielder Braiden Ward.
Veteran catcher Tomas Nido has also come up from Worcester to serve as an extra catcher on the taxi squad for the Red Sox.
Extra innings
The Red Sox announced Eli White underwent successful Lisfranc repair surgery on his right foot Tuesday. The procedure was performed by Dr. Martin O’Malley at the Hospital for Special Surgery in New York City. … Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) is feeling much better but is still a day or two away from a return to the mound. … Curtis Mead (fractured left wrist) has resumed swinging a regular bat and is taking overhand batting practice, but while the Red Sox haven’t ruled out a possible return, Tracy acknowledged that time isn’t on his side.

item.content:encoded:
Once again, Garrett Crochet donned a full Red Sox uniform, made the walk from the bullpen to the mound, and pitched at Fenway Park on Tuesday afternoon. This time, he faced a live hitter -- in the form of Ceddanne Rafaela -- as he took another step toward returning to the mound for Boston.
And for the first time in what's been a long recovery period, the 27-year-old said he feels ready to contribute.
"I would say, the way that that live [batting practice] just went, that I could go get outs," Crochet told reporters inside the Red Sox clubhouse.
That being said, Crochet shared that he has some hesitance to joining the roster, though it has nothing to do with his own health.
"This team's had a great year. I think that for me to take a spot on the roster, then someone would have to lose one. And I would feel bad doing that, because this team has pitched their ass off the whole season," Crochet said. "Ultimately, that's something that's gonna be up to the front office. And whenever they gauge that I'm ready, then I'll accept that. In the meantime, I'm just gonna keep working my butt off."
More Red Sox Coverage
Crochet's work on Tuesday involved 16 pitches, and he estimated he was sitting at 94-96 mph on his fastball velocity. The left-hander said how well he recovers on Wednesday will be a significant determinant on his ability to pitch in games. Yet when asked if he'll pitch in a regular-season game this weekend or save his return for the postseason, he is leaving that decision to chief baseball officer Craig Breslow and manager Chad Tracy.
"I think that I'm just gonna do whatever they tell me to do, to be honest," he said. "I think that [live BPs] and games, obviously it's a big step up and the pressure of the moment, I suppose, and the intensity. But I don't think that there's a set amount of [live BPs] that need to be thrown before a game."
Tracy, who officially dropped the interim tag earlier in the day, said that whatever decision is made on Crochet, it will be "done with Garrett's best interests in mind."
"Looking at what is he able to accomplish this week, and what does the playoffs require?" Tracy explained. "And then deciding can he fit that role or not based on what he's done."
Ceddanne Rafaela
Rafaela, who hasn't played since Sept. 2 due to a hamstring injury, partook in the live BP with Crochet as he nears a return to the lineup.
"Much better," Tracy said on Rafaela. "Getting close there."
Rafaela has produced the best offensive season of his career, as he's batted .282 with a .760 OPS in 135 games, while continuing to provide Gold Glove-level defense in center field.
Willson Contreras
Tracy also shared a positive injury update on Willson Contreras, who continues to improve after taking a pitch off his right hand last Thursday.
Tracy said that Contreras is "doing much better" and is "swinging aggressively" as he works his way back to full strength.
Aroldis Chapman
Closer Aroldis Chapman hasn't pitched since Sept. 13 due to some lat tightness, but Tracy had yet another positive injury update.
"He's getting very close," Tracy said. "I think we're a day or two away from him being ready to roll."
Group staying ready in Fort Myers
The Red Sox are keeping a team of reinforcements ready in Fort Myers for the playoff run, in case anybody is needed as an injury replacement along the way. That list of players includes:
- SP Tanner Houck
- SP Johan Oviedo
- SS/2B Franklin Arias
- OF Braiden Ward
- RP Wyatt Olds
- SS/2B Tsung-Che Cheng
- RP Tyler Samaniego
- 1B/2B Romy Gonzalez
- RP Jedixson Paez
Curtis Mead
Perhaps the lone negative injury update from Tracy was on second baseman Curtis Mead, who broke his wrist in his first game with the Red Sox on July 27.
"Haven't ruled it out yet. It's gonna be tough," Tracy said when asked if Mead might be able to return for the first round of the playoffs.
Tracy said that Mead is taking some overhand batting practice, but there may not be enough time for Mead to progress to being game-ready.
"I said we would probably be a little aggressive to see how the hand responds," Tracy said. "Have not ruled it out. It's just we're getting up against it a bit."

For the most part, the Red Sox know who their key contributors will be in the AL Wild Card round. But on Tuesday, fans got positive updates on two injured stars, both of whom appear to be nearing potential returns.
Here's the latest on both Garrett Crochet and Curtis Mead as they work toward getting back to full health for the Red Sox.
Red Sox Get Encouraging Signs From Two Injured Stars Ahead of Postseason
Boston's pitching staff has been terrific in 2026 despite the absence of Crochet, who has been out since April with a lat strain and other shoulder inflammation. But ahead of the postseason, it appears Crochet is ramping up at a perfect time.
Crochet throwing live BP with Ceddanne at Fenway today 👀 pic.twitter.com/Iwv2R14iVk
— NESN (@NESN) September 22, 2026
On Tuesday, Crochet was seen completing a live BP session against Ceddanne Rafaela, throwing 16 pitches that included a velocity in the 94-96 mph range, according to Tyler Milliken.
Garrett Crochet ended up throwing a total of 16 pitches in his first live BP.
Velocity was in the 94-96 range. Few ticks up from the last time he threw a regular bullpen. Currently feeling good and thinks he can get outs.
Some great video from @alexspeier. pic.twitter.com/ZMsMmUXzvU
Notably, per Chris Cotillo, Crochet also told reporters that he thinks he could "get outs" with the way his live session went.
On Saturday, new full-time manager Chad Tracy also provided the latest on Crochet and whether he could return, potentially as a reliever for the postseason.
“I think it just depends on how he feels coming out of it, how much volume we give him,” Tracy said, per MLB.com. “So it’s hard to say. I know it’s not a great answer, but it’s just really how it is. How does he feel after each step? So when he does that, how does he feel? And then determine from there. Do we give him more hitters or do we want to put him in a game? It’s hard to say until you know how he feels.
Meanwhile, infielder Curtis Mead, who was injured in his Red Sox debut in July, also appeared to take a step forward on Tuesday. According to Cotillo, Mead, at one point during Crochet's session, appeared to be getting ready to step into the batter's box as well. Over the weekend, Mead began hitting off a tee and playing catch, per MLB.com.
There's no guarantee that Crochet or Mead will be ready in time for a likely best-of-three playoff series, but either could provide Boston with a huge boost. At their best, Crochet is one of baseball's best left-handed pitchers, while Mead hit 17 home runs before joining the Red Sox this season.

The Boston Red Sox thought they had made a solid early splash well ahead of the MLB trade deadline when they acquired Curtis Mead from the Washington Nationals for lefty pitcher Connelly Early.
Instead, Mead was injured in his first game playing for the Red Sox, and he hasn’t appeared in a game since.
With the playoffs beginning next week, Mead has mostly run out of time to return, but there are starting to be hints that he could soon be back on the field.
Curtis Mead Injury Update
On Tuesday, for example, Mead was digging in to take an at bat against Garrett Crochet, the lefty ace who is also on his way back from injury.
Live at bats are a big step in a comeback, so this is quite encouraging:
Rafaela is in the box now and it looks like Curtis Mead is next, which is interesting.
— Chris Cotillo (@ChrisCotillo) September 22, 2026
It had actually been reported over the weekend that Mead had begun doing some work off a tee, which is an early step.
He’s coming back from a fractured left wrist, so it’ll be all about getting his hands and hitting mechanics to feel right.
Curtis Mead Stats
Mead was awesome for Washington this season before being traded.
He had played 87 games, and he had an .852 OPS in that time. He had doubled 17 times, hit a triple and left the yard with 17 home runs. Mead had 48 RBI and 49 runs for the Nats, and also had stolen six bases in eight attempts.
It was by far his most production in the major leagues. In 90 games in the 2025 season split between the Rays and White Sox, Mead had just three homers. In the two seasons prior to that, Mead had appeared in 52 games for the Rays and hit a total of two home runs.
This season, though, the shine he once had as a pretty promising prospect showed itself for Mead.
The Nationals didn’t have to trade Mead. He’s under club control through 2030.
Washington simply didn’t want to pass up the opportunity to get an arm like Early.
The Red Sox, on the flip side, wanted more right-handed hitting production out of the infield, where Mead can play multiple positions.
Mead will have future seasons to prove it to be a good trade for Boston, but it remains to be seen whether he’ll return in time this year to start making that case.
At least Mead seems to be taking steps in the right direction. Still just 25, the native of Australia would be eligible to impact the pennant race if the Red Sox want to activate him. Maybe if he looks good taking some live at bats, Mead will make a quality case for himself.

Even with the Red Sox having secured their second straight postseason berth, the magnitude of Craig Breslow’s gamble five months ago remains startling.
There have been times when teams reacted to slow starts with a managerial or coaching staff change. But longtime members of the industry could not recall anything like the shakeup enacted by Breslow in April, when he fired manager Alex Cora and replaced six other members of the coaching staff.
It was a move that departed from convention both for when it happened (barely a month into the season) and the extent of the change. It also pointed to an emerging theme of Breslow’s time as chief baseball officer: The willingness of the Sox to take significant in-season risks.
The firing of Cora and the staff members (with replacements plucked from the minors with little big league clubhouse experience), the mid-June trade of Rafael Devers in 2025, and the acquisition of catcher Adley Rutschman in exchange for a package of young talent (four of the Sox’ top 10 prospects, as well as catcher Carlos Narváez) that exceeded any in-season move by the Sox this century all pointed to an organization making massive bets on in-season changes.
“I always try to be guided by what I believe to be right and best for the organization,” Breslow said of his in-season risk tolerance. “Oftentimes, most people in these jobs would say their initial read or inclination of a situation was largely a correct one, but friction and inertia and emotion prevented you from acting on that. Then, you look back and say I wish I would have done whatever it was you were thinking at the time more often than you say that was probably not the right decision, and I wish I hadn’t.
“When you evaluate decisions through that lens, I think I default to, when you reach a certain level of conviction, you have to act.”
That sounds straightforward, but given baseball’s 162-game schedule, there’s often a willingness by heads of baseball operations to let situations play out over larger samples rather than intervene quickly. On both a personal and organizational level, a major in-season shakeup is uncomfortable.
“I certainly don’t sleep well [after a major change] for a few reasons, mostly because these are people that you have relationships with, and it’s not the outcome that you were looking for,” said Breslow. “These decisions are incredibly difficult. We’re talking about people’s lives, their families, children … there are a lot of implications to making these changes. So, it is wildly uncomfortable.”
Still, in a view perhaps informed by his playing career, Breslow has learned to remain open to uncomfortable in-season change — not for its own sake, but instead as a course correction when he sees a path to improving the club.
“I try to balance my [playing] experiences with what more information is telling me,” Breslow said. “I don’t think if I were only looking through things as I had experienced them that that would necessarily position us to make better decisions. But I think ignoring them would be ignoring valuable insights that I’ve learned.
“I was a lefthanded reliever that bounced around, who didn’t find success early on, pretty consistently evaluated the information that my performance was telling me, and tried to make adjustments as quickly as possible. I didn’t have the luxury of infinite runway in front of me to figure things out over time. If that’s an attitude or approach that I take to this job, then I think that’s OK.”
Breslow’s playing career may also inform his approach to in-season risks in another way: The way he values the chance to contend for a title.
It certainly would have been understandable if the Sox had decided by mid-June — around their 32-46 nadir — that they were open for business in a sell-off. Indeed, the Sox were at least starting to prepare for such an eventuality, with some of their pro scouts assigned to organizations who might be interested in short-term veterans, particularly Sonny Gray (who will be a free agent after 2026).
That said, Breslow had experience as a player of a long-shot team emerging as a champion. And so, even though there were few precedents for a team such as the Sox to overcome their long odds, based on his belief in the talent of the group, Breslow wanted to give the team as much time as possible to compete, respecting what he referred to as “the sanctity of a season.”
“Maybe that is born out of my playing career and the fact that the Red Sox won the World Series in 2013 as an improbable group going into the season,” he said. “Fundamentally, my confidence and belief in the players that we had on our roster [in 2026] had not changed. Players didn’t become meaningfully less talented. My belief in the roster was consistent.”
“But it’s interesting. Everybody who sits in my seat is going to talk about sustainability and the ability to compete for championships every single year. I think it’s very important to balance that with acknowledging the importance of every individual season. Otherwise, you talk about windows and about how maybe this isn’t the year, but that’s OK because next year we’ll still have the core of a really good team.
“I have learned that sometimes really good teams don’t have the seasons that they want. Sometimes teams that you don’t have maybe the highest expectations far outperform them for a season’s length. So you don’t want to dismiss what is immediately in front of you in exchange for this idea of lumping seasons together and just kind of thinking about being in the midst of a window.”
And so, the Sox ended up doing the opposite of what everyone forecast. A team for whom a veteran sell-off seemed almost inevitable instead ended up — thanks to one of the great runs in franchise history from late June to mid-August — taking big swings for deadline upgrades with moves to add infielder Curtis Mead and Rutschman.
In different ways, both moves stunned the industry given what the Sox gave up (Connelly Early for Mead; prospects Anthony Eyanson, Kyson Witherspoon, Enddy Azocar, and Harold Rivas, as well as Narváez for Rutschman). But from afar, Rangers president of baseball operations Chris Young — like Breslow, a former player — could appreciate what his colleague did.
“In general, careers are short, and I want every player that puts on our uniform to have a chance to compete for a World Series. That should be our goal as an organization,” said Young. “When you have a team that’s in a win cycle, you need to be bold at times to go for it.
“It doesn’t mean necessarily you’re going to sustain success, but the goal is not to just make the playoffs. The goal is to win championships. And for me, especially in 2023 when we made very bold moves, it led to [a championship]. It easily could not have, but I know that if we didn’t make those moves, we wouldn’t have won. [And] there’s no doubt the player in me is influenced by the opportunity to win.”
Breslow’s deadline deals were motivated by a similar hunger. Now that the Red Sox have qualified for the playoffs, the ultimate impact of the bets made by Breslow in what he repeatedly described as a “difficult” season will gain greater definition in the postseason tournament.
But regardless of what happens, the path to get to the playoffs represented a fascinating shift in how the Red Sox conducted business, in a fashion that defied expectations at numerous turns on and off the field.

item.content:encoded:
If you're not already a card collector, Red Sox fans, here's the quick version of what product sports cards enthusiasts are going crazy over right now. Bowman Chrome is Topps' flagship prospect release, the one product every year built specifically around getting a player's first-ever card into the hobby before he's played a single big-league game. Think of it like a company's IPO. It's the first moment the public gets to invest or collect a piece of a player’s career, before anyone really knows what it'll become.
That's the appeal, and it's also the risk. Some of these names turn into stars. Some never sniff the majors at all. Either way, this is the top of the sports card market right now, and some of these prices have gotten astronomical. You have to truly believe in these prospects to justify what you're paying for a shot at them.
The 1st Bowman class, Roman Anthony rookie cards, and how to collect Red Sox legends
Boston has four 1st Bowman cards this year, all likely the cheapest they’ll ever be simply because nobody outside the organization and minor league baseball enthusiasts know most of these names yet. Here's a rough rule of thumb worth keeping in mind: the higher the signing bonus, the more attention collectors tend to pay, and that logic really kicks in once a bonus crosses $750,000. If a front office was willing to bet that kind of money on a teenager's upside, it's a fair question why a collector wouldn't take the same signal seriously.
Dawvris Brito signed for $1.2 million as the headliner of the 2026 international class, a shortstop with quick-twitch athleticism and triple-digit exit velocities already, and if there is a speculative play, I’d be playing in Brito’s camp. Garielvin Silverio signed for $1.4 million as a physical, left-handed-hitting corner outfielder with raw power, but is likely limited to a corner outfield spot due to lack of speed and athleticism.
Louis Andujar is the wild card of the group, and exactly the kind of story that makes chasing a bargain fun. Boston signed him for just $20,000 out of the Dominican Republic, a number so modest he barely registered outside the organization. He quietly hit .280 with a .974 OPS in the Dominican Summer League, then hit .410 with a 1.233 OPS in his stateside debut this year, good enough for FCL Hitter of the Week honors. If the $750,000 rule (that I made up completely) tells you who the industry believes in, Andujar is the opposite bet entirely, a near-free flier already outplaying his price tag.
The last name in this class comes with the best story attached. Enddy Azocar signed with Boston in January 2024 for just $40,000 out of Venezuela. He climbed all the way to the Red Sox's No. 5 prospect by this summer, hitting .286 with 18 home runs and 11 stolen bases in 85 games, right before Boston shipped him to Baltimore in the Rutschman trade. He hasn't missed a beat since, hitting .467 with a 1.238 OPS in his first 15 at-bats for High-A Frederick, and he's now the Orioles' No. 8 prospect. His 1st Bowman card will always have a Red Sox jersey, a snapshot of the last piece of a $40,000 bet Boston made and then dealt away for a franchise catcher.
Connelly Early carries that same wrinkle in a smaller way. Boston shipped him to the Nationals this July in the Curtis Mead deal, yet his Red RC in this release still has him in a Red Sox uniform. If you're a true Red Sox fan who likes owning a piece of the ones that got away, these are exactly those cards.
If you’re a top prospect hunter and have slept on Franklin Arias, this release gives you more chances to buy into his market, just not the way you'd expect. He doesn't get a 1st Bowman card this year (his 1st came last year), but he shows up with a prospect auto and two inserts as one of the sport's top prospects. If his original 1st Bowman wave passed you by, this is a more affordable way back into his market before he's an everyday big leaguer.
If you believe in Roman Anthony, the rest of this checklist is built for you. This year has been riddled with injury, a hand issue that kept him out for months. But zoom out. Boston signed this guy to an eight-year, $130 million extension back in August 2025, running through 2033 with a 2034 option and escalators that could push the value to $230 million.
That's a franchise betting on a 22-year-old being the face of this roster for the next decade, and Anthony's Red RC, Chrome Rookie Auto, Jumbo Chrome Autograph Relic, and Across the Seams autograph all reflect that same belief. If you're the kind of collector who buys into a player rather than a single season, the injury noise shouldn't scare you off so much as it should make this exact window the moment to buy in, before he's healthy and the price reflects it.
Every team in this release gets a shot at the future. Not every team has the history and memories that Red Sox fans have and names like Manny Ramirez, Roger Clemens, and Pedro Martínez in the same checklist should be like a slice of heaven. Ramirez lands in the Bowman Garbage Pail Kids (GPK) insert, a fitting nod to one of the most feared right-handed bats this franchise has ever run out. Clemens goes a step further with a base GPK card and an autograph version, and Pedro shows up in the Final Draft insert. None of these are prospect chases, and none will likely come cheap either, but they're closer to a tribute set than an investment. For a fanbase that grew up on these names, that's a fun thing to pull, regardless of cost.
Prices are always inflated in the first few weeks. Anthony's cards will likely cost the most, so waiting a month for the market to settle isn't unreasonable if you're patient. But Brito, Silverio, Azocar, and Andujar are cheap speculative buys worth grabbing now, and the Manny, Clemens, and Pedro pulls are worth paying up for if the fun of the rip matters more to you than the price tag.

The Boston Red Sox are just a few wins from clinching a playoff spot for the second year in a row following a three-year hiatus. It's been a successful year on paper for the Red Sox, especially given all of their early-season chaos. But it's hard not to wonder... what if this team had been healthier in 2026?
Deadline acquisition Curtis Mead barely got to play at all for the Red Sox, and now he could be done for the season. Garrett Crochet made just six starts for Boston. Roman Anthony lost the bulk of what was supposed to be his first full MLB season. Justin Slaten's season is now over prematurely.
Everywhere you look on Boston's '26 roster, there are questions about what could have been. Mead is a potent right-handed bat who was supposed to add not only extra thump to the lineup but also infield depth.
Crochet is a much bigger theoretical. Last year's AL Cy Young runner-up pitched just 30 innings for Boston this season before landing on the IL with shoulder inflammation. In essence, the Red Sox rotation has been missing its true ace for nearly the entire year.
Red Sox's 2026 season comes with a huge "What if?"
Anthony’s absence was also tough to swallow for months. He hit .292/.396/.463 with an 140 OPS+ in 71 games as a 21-year-old in 2025, leading many to crown him Boston's franchise player moving forward. This year he played 30 games, then tore a ligament in his right ring finger on a check swing in early May. It was a freak injury that a hand specialist told reporters he had never seen isolated that way.
The Red Sox couldn't have expected Anthony to miss as much time as he did, and the somewhat mysterious nature of the injury made it impossible to plan for when he'd come back. It was a perpetual "when's he coming back?" buzzkill situation for the organization and its fans for months, not that Anthony is to blame.
Anthony and Crochet's absences alone make one wonder if the Red Sox would have already clinched by now had those two been healthy for most of the season. Certainly the Wild Card, no? The division is a harder argument, based on how good Tampa Bay has been all year. But we can realistically assume that the Red Sox would at least be battling the Yankees for the wild-card lead right now (or better) had Anthony and Crochet played more games.
Alas, that's all water under the bridge, and this roster is still on track for October baseball, thanks to a historic surge after the All-Star break. This is a more patched-together version of the Red Sox than any Boston fan would have preferred, but such is often the consequence of a 162-game marathon. Even so, no matter how Boston fares in the postseason (outside of a run to the World Series), fans will always be asking "What if?" about this year.

Curtis Mead has arguably been the most frustrating non-factor for the Boston Red Sox this season, because he never got his chance to make an impact.
In his very first game after being acquired in a trade with the Washington Nationals, Mead fractured his left wrist on a high-and-tight fastball against the Athletics. He quickly found himself in an uphill battle to return to action before the Red Sox's season ended at some point in the playoffs, but he's started making some progress.
According to a Saturday MLB.com injury update, Mead has begun hitting off a tee, which slipped under the radar amid a slough of injury news about Willson Contreras, Garrett Crochet, and others. Good news, to be sure, but far from a guarantee he makes it back for a game this year.
Mead's return not imminent, but progress made
Interim manager Chad Tracy said earlier this week that the tee work was beginning on Wednesday, per Boston Sports Gordo on X. That means we're a few days late to this particular story, so apologies to our readers — but not much slips by us, so it was a particularly quiet announcement.
Mead's breakout season (.851 OPS, 17 home runs in 88 games) was halted at the worst possible time. The Red Sox were looking to add an impact bat at the trade deadline, and Mead's absence has been nearly as awkward as Adley Rutschman's struggles.
Would Mead be the slam-dunk starter at second base even if he came back fully healthy this week? That's another real issue to consider, since Nick Sogard has done a nice job over the last month-plus. Perhaps Mead would at least be in the lineup against left-handed pitchers over the struggling Andruw Monasterio and/or Isiah Kiner-Falefa.
The Red Sox will have interesting decisions to make at the fringes of the roster for the first couple of rounds of the playoffs, no matter what. If Mead re-enters the picture, we could see someone who feels like they earned their spot get the axe, but that's the cost of doing business in a year when the American League could be up for grabs.

item.content:encoded:
Can you believe the playoffs are almost here? A week from today the Red Sox will wrap up their regular season, closing the book on what has been among the most unexpected, topsy turvy seasons we’ve ever seen. From there the playoffs await, and who knows what twists and turns may still be in store.
But before we get there, what business is there left for the Red Sox to get squared away before Game 1 of the Wild Card series? We answer your questions in today’s Red Sox mailbag.
Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet both appear close to ready to return. What is the chance that the Red Sox decide to put both of them on the postseason roster? Each feels like a high upside question mark but is it too risky relying on both of them to excel in limited roles? — Paul from Bluesky
If the Red Sox decide they’re ready I think there’s a great chance both pitch in the playoffs. The question of whether or not it’s too risky is valid, but the other factor to consider is would it be riskier to let an inferior arm take the mound at Yankee Stadium with the season on the line.
The nature of a best-of-three playoff series compared to a best-of-five or even a best-of-seven also makes the idea of loading up on short-inning relievers more attractive.
The Red Sox will only need three starting pitchers in the first round, presumably Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle, in some order. That effectively frees up two additional bullpen spots, one of which I’m guessing will be filled by Jake Bennett as an emergency bulk man should the starter exit early due to injury or poor performance.
The back end of the bullpen is pretty much set in stone. If everyone is healthy and available it will be Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Erik Miller and Tyron Guerrero locking down the high leverage innings. But after that the Red Sox have some interesting decisions to make.
In one group you have the other short men, including Greg Weissert, Jovani Moran and Wyatt Olds. Then in the next group you have the longer men, including Patrick Sandoval, Brayan Bello, Alec Gamboa and Raymond Burgos. Finally, you have Crochet, Houck and Johan Oviedo, who has also begun a rehab assignment after missing nearly the entire season. What the Red Sox have to decide is which five of those 10 options give you the best chance to win?
I don’t think you can dispute that Crochet and Houck have the highest ceiling of that bunch, so if they’re good to go I don’t think the Red Sox will hesitate to give them the nod.
With Romy Gonzalez now hitting so well in Worcester, do you see him being put on the postseason roster as a lefty masher, and one of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Jahmai Jones being left off? — @wcbosox on Bluesky
If the Red Sox believe Romy Gonzalez gives them the best chance to win in October, I feel like it would make sense for them to call him up and get him some looks at big league pitching over the last two weeks. You could make a great case that they should — he was batting .360 in 23 games since being optioned to Triple-A entering Friday — but if that doesn’t happen then that could be a sign the Red Sox don’t see him as part of the October plan.
Either way, the club has some tough decisions to make as far as constructing the bench goes.
Presuming that Ceddanne Rafaela returns from the IL without any issues and Willson Contreras isn’t sidelined by his hand injury, the Red Sox should enter the playoffs with a starting lineup featuring Adley Rutschman at catcher, Contreras, Nick Sogard, Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin across the infield, and an outfield of Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Roman Anthony and Jarren Duran, with one of Anthony or Duran presumably starting at designated hitter if a righty is on the mound.
That leaves four spots for Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio, Jones, Mickey Gasper, Connor Wong, Nate Eaton, Gonzalez and possibly Curtis Mead. For our purposes we can probably set aside Eaton, who will likely be optioned upon Rafaela’s activation, as well as Mead, who only just started swinging a light bat and won’t have the benefit of a rehab assignment prior to his return.
Let’s also set aside some of the more outside the box candidates like Braiden Ward, who has never appeared in a big league game but who may garner consideration as a late-inning pinch runner after stealing 60 bases at Triple-A.
One spot will go to a backup catcher, and while you could talk yourself into Gasper filling that role, Wong has the most familiarity with the pitching staff and the Red Sox would probably rather keep Gasper available as a pinch hitter without worrying about catching logistics.
How about the other three spots? Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio and Gonzalez are all versatile infield defenders who bat right-handed, so there’s some redundancy there. Jones also bats right-handed and could function as an emergency reserve outfielder in addition to his pinch hitter, and while Gasper is technically a switch hitter, his real value comes from the left side, where he’s crushed righties over the past month.
What’s going to happen? My guess is the bench will be Wong, Gasper, Jones and one of the three righty infielders. So to go back to your original question, could Gonzalez make the playoff roster over one of Kiner-Falefa, Monasterio or Jones? Yes, and in fact even if he doesn’t make the roster one of those guys could still wind up on the outside looking in.
If the playoffs started today who would be the starting second baseman? Also, what’s the long-term plan for that position? — Tom P.
If the playoffs started today I think Nick Sogard would be the clear choice to start at second base. He’s been an everyday player for the Red Sox since the end of July, and at a time where most of the offense has hit a skid Sogard has been a reliable contributor at the plate, batting .262 with five home runs and a .772 OPS entering the weekend since being called back up on July 29.
Long-term, the Red Sox have a couple of different candidates who could emerge in the coming years.
If he hadn’t broken his wrist in his team debut I think it’s safe to say Curtis Mead would have spent the past two months starting at second for the Red Sox. Prior to the trade he was in the midst of a breakout season with the Washington Nationals, and at only 25 years old there’s good reason to believe his best years are still ahead of him. Whether he returns in the playoffs or for the start of next season, Mead should have the best chance to claim second base for himself.
But outside of him, Sogard and perhaps Gonzalez or Anthony Seigler, there is one other wild card. That’s Franklin Arias.
The top Red Sox prospect is putting the finishing touches on a brilliant season, and if he continues to develop he should have a great chance of becoming a key building block, perhaps as soon as next year. With Story under contract for only one more season he will have an opportunity to slide right into the starting shortstop job entering 2028, but what if he proves he’s ready for primetime before that? In that case Arias might get an initial look at second, with Mead perhaps rotating between the designated hitter spot and occasionally giving Durbin and Contreras a breather at their corner infield positions.
Does MLB need to readjust its postseason schedule? The No. 2 or 3 team in the American League will be eliminated in a three-game series, meanwhile two teams that are barely .500 play each other in the first round. — Brandon C.
I like the idea that there should be a reward for winning your division. If you’re one of the top two division winners you get a first round bye, and if you’re the third division winner you at least get to host the best-of-three Wild Card series. I’m fine with that, even in a weird year like this where all of the American League’s best teams are in the same division and the other division leaders are mediocre at best.
But the problem is what happens afterwards. Like you said, the No. 2 and 3 teams in the AL are probably going to wind up being the Yankees and Red Sox, and whichever of those teams advances will have to play the No. 1 seeded Tampa Bay Rays. Meanwhile, all three teams on the other side of the bracket could potentially finish with worse records than anyone on the AL East side, and one of those clubs will be guaranteed a trip to the ALCS.
I think MLB could address this by reseeding after the Wild Card round. The top two division winners would still get home field advantage in their divisional series, but whichever team advancing out of the Wild Card round has the better record would be paired with the second division winner. So this year if the Red Sox beat the Yankees and let’s say the AL West champion wins their Wild Card series, the Red Sox would go on to play the AL Central champion instead of the Rays, while the AL West champion would get Tampa Bay even though they would have technically started the playoffs as the higher seed.
Most years it probably won’t make a huge difference, but reseeding ahead of the divisional round would strike a balance between preserving the incentives for winning your division while ensuring the bracket doesn’t become unbalanced.

Red Sox Insert Jahmai Jones into Lineup Against Rays Lefty
The Boston Red Sox placed designated hitter Jahmai Jones in the third spot in the starting lineup on Friday against Tampa Bay Rays left-hander Ian Seymour at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida.
According to MLB.com, Jones sits in the heart of the order between outfielders Roman Anthony and Wilyer Abreu. Shortstop Trevor Story and first baseman Nick Sogard also feature in the top five positions for Boston.
Left-hander Ranger Suárez gets the start on the mound for Boston against Tampa Bay's Seymour. Seymour enters the contest holding a 9-6 record with a 4.27 ERA and 150 strikeouts on the season, according to official team statistics.
Boston manager Chad Tracy opted to stack the right-handed hitting Jones near the top of the batting order due to ongoing injuries and lack of availability among several key players, including Ceddanne Rafaela, Masataka Yoshida, Curtis Mead, and Willson Contreras.
According to MLB Trade Rumors, Boston acquired Jones off waivers on July 14 after the Detroit Tigers designated him for assignment, sending pitching prospect Jojo Ingrassia to Detroit as compensation.
Jones struggled with Detroit this season, batting .137 with a .221 slugging percentage across 105 plate appearances before his release. However, he has turned his season around in Boston, slashing .362/.464/.681 with three home runs and eight RBIs in 56 plate appearances.
Friday marks the 20th time overall this season that Jones has occupied the third spot in a starting lineup, having done so 19 times prior across his stints with Detroit and Boston. In those previous 35 plate appearances in the third spot, he posted a .219 batting average and a .661 OPS.
According to FanGraphs, the platoon splits support Boston's heavy usage of Jones against left-handed pitching. Across 138 plate appearances against lefties this year, Jones has recorded a .223 batting average, a .333 on-base percentage, and a .420 slugging percentage with five home runs, 15 walks, and 14 RBIs.
Conversely, Jones has registered just a .130 average in 23 at-bats against right-handed pitchers, with all five of his home runs this season coming exclusively against left-handers. He previously hit a two-run home run off Seymour during a July 18 matchup at Fenway Park.
Boston enters the three-game series against the American League East-leading Rays with an 83-70 record, holding the second AL Wild Card position and a five-game lead over the Cleveland Guardians. Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.

According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to carry the momentum from Thursday's come-from-behind win into the final road series of the year against the Rays. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) will get the start for the Red Sox opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for the Rays. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

The Boston Red Sox will not have Willson Contreras in the lineup on Friday night against the Tampa Bay Rays, but there is hope for the All-Star slugger after an early exit on Thursday night.
Contreras had to leave the club's series finale against the Texas Rangers on Thursday night after getting hit by a pitch on his hand. At the time, it was reported that his X-rays came back negative, but there was still some fear. Contreras himself spoke about the injury and said that it felt like a fracture while citing the fact that he previously had one.
Now, of course, it would've been great to see Contreras in Boston's lineup on Friday, but he hasn't been ruled out for the weekend and Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that no new scans are currently planned, as shared on X by MassLive.com's Sean McAdam.
Willson Contreras Update
"Willson Contreras is out of the lineup, giving his hand some time to recover. Chad Tracy wouldn’t rule him out for the weekend, but Sox are being cautious. No new scans planned," McAdam wrote on X.
Again, it would've been great to see Contreras back in the lineup, but there are positives to take away from this update. First and foremost, the fact that more scans aren't currently planned is a sign of confidence from the club. Think back to Curtis Mead, for example. When he got hit on the wrist in his first game as a member of the Red Sox, his X-rays initially came back as negative. Then, the next day, it was shared that he actually had suffered a fractured wrist.
At this point, every time someone gets hit by a pitch on the wrist/hand, it immediately makes fans think about Mead. This process with Contreras is much more positive than it was with Mead. The fact that almost 24 hours later, the club hasn't ruled him out for the weekend and doesn't have more tests planned is a very good sign that he simply is dealing with a bruise, or something of that nature.
Boston needs Contreras if it wants to make a run this season. Things are wide open in the American League, especially in the wake of Aaron Judge being placed on the Injured List for the New York Yankees. Boston, New York and Tampa Bay are the top three contenders in the American League and with New York hurting, the top two contenders should be the Red Sox and the Rays. If Contreras returns over the weekend, Boston is going to be just fine.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras gets hit by a lot of pitches — he's been hit 24 times in 129 games this year, tying his career high — but the one on September 17 was different. Contreras mostly takes his base without issue, occasionally chirping pitchers and trying to rally his teammates on the way, but it was obvious something was wrong this time.
In the top of the eighth inning, a pitch from Texas Rangers pitcher Jakob Junis knocked Contreras in the hand. The first baseman hit the ground and immediately shook out his hand in pain. He walked off the field with a trainer uncharacteristically fast, which only worsened fans' nerves.
Postgame x-rays of Contreras' hand came back clear of any breaks but he's still experiencing pain (according to Chris Cotillo of MassLive). Contreras is less convinced by the results of the imaging. He told reporters he thinks his hand is fractured and that it went numb for a time after the hit (via Tim Healey of The Boston Globe).
The Red Sox have classified Contreras as day-to-day, but his reaction coupled with the club's history of evaluating injuries has some people doubting the diagnosis. The situation is reminiscent of what happened with Curtis Mead.
Willson Contreras' pain level seemingly outweighing initial diagnosis is giving Red Sox fans Curtis Mead flashbacks
A pitch plunked Mead on the wrist in his second at-bat as a Red Sox following the team's acquisition at the trade deadline. Initial imaging came back clear. The following day, he underwent a more detailed scan that revealed a wrist fracture. The fracture was non-displaced, meaning the broken part of his wrist remained aligned so he didn't have to undergo surgery to repair it, but his wrist is fractured all the same.
The Red Sox had better hope their initial diagnosis is correct this time. Losing Contreras for any amount of time, even with a day-to-day diagnosis, is a brutal outcome for the Sox. He's fresh off the injured list after a nearly two-week stint with a hamstring issue and he expects to be sidelined again for at least a few days.
Contreras has been Boston's most important bat all season and his career-high 27 home runs lead the team. The Red Sox need Contreras at his best for their playoff run, but if his hand is injured in any way, "his best" may be out the window.
Hopefully Contreras' initial diagnosis is right and Boston doesn't have another Mead situation on its hands. Contreras has been too important to the Red Sox's offense all season and his leadership is too valuable to lose him long-term at such a critical time, but the injury bug doesn't bite at ideal times.

If the Boston Red Sox are going to make a deep playoff run this season, they're going to need first baseman Willson Contreras at his best. Unfortunately, he is up in the air rigth now after leaving Thursday's contest early against the Texas Rangers.
Contreras stepped up to the plate in the eighth inning on Thursday night and was hit on the top of the hand and was in clear discomfort right away and quickly exited the game and was replaced by Isiah Kiner-Falefa as a pinch runner.
After the game, Contreras shared an update about the injury, as transcribed by MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo.
"Sore. Painful," Contreras said. "My hand was numb for like five minutes. That was the reason I came out of the game. I have fractured, before, the same hand. It felt like a fracture. Thankfully, it’s not a fracture on the top of the bone. I’m just frustrated."
When your most consistent hitter has any sort of injury scare with under two weeks to go until the playoffs, that's something that warrants some nerves in the fanbase, especially when the offense has been struggling. The fact that he specifically said that he had a fracture before and that it felt the same added to the fears. On the bright side, he underwent an X-ray that initially came back negative. Still, he's not fully out of the water yet.
Best-Case Scenario
In a perfect world, the pain subsides for Contreras and he's able to return to the field on Friday night on the road against the Tampa Bay Rays with just a bruise. Or, at the very least, he's able to play at some point during the series against Tampa Bay.
It's not hard to see why this would be the best-case scenario. Contreras has played in 129 games and is slashing .276/.387/.518 with a .905 OPS, 27 homers, 81 RBIs, and 21 doubles. Plus, he's at 4.6 wins above replacement. The quicker he can get back, the better. He already underwent an X-ray that had good news. Now, it all comes down to how it feels when he wakes. Hopefully, when the swelling goes down, it doesn't reveal any more issues.
Worst-Case Scenario
For the worst-case scenario, look no further than Curtis Mead. When Mead initially got hit by a pitch on his hand back in July, his X-rays initially came back negative. Then, after further testing, it was revealed that he actually suffered a fractured wrist. Mead hasn't played in a game since and it's unclear if the Red Sox will get him before the season comes to a close.
The worst-case scenario for Contreras would be something similar happening. As the swelling goes down, if it were to reveal some sort of fracture as well, that would be bad news for his chances of a quick return.

This is why we watch! Trevor Story's season looked dead and buried both three months and three weeks ago. He's battled injury, surgery, rehab, way too many strikeouts, and growing chatter from knuckleheads like me who have repeatedly questioned if he even belongs back in this lineup.
Well tonight, he came to the plate with the Sox down 3-1 in the eighth and on the verge of getting swept. He was facing a tough reliever in Jacob Latz, a Texas team that was 63-1 when leading after seven innings, and the weight of his team going a combined 0-17 with runners in scoring position in the series up to that point.
Then he did this:
As somebody that's been leading the "Trevor Story is cooked " charges, I love this so much! Nothing can humble and amaze quite like baseball, and after months of hard work, grinding behind the scenes, and having to deal with all the noise, Story smashed a 108mph line drive home run not only in the face of Latz and Texas' playoff hopes, but also in the face of all those who have been doubting him for weeks (hand raised).
It's just one game, and the real test doesn't start until the 29th, but boy did this have to feel incredible for Story who hadn't gone deep since May 13th. To do it in that moment, in his home town, and against the backdrop of everything that's happened this year is just so perfectly baseball. It's why we love this game so much, and why people like Story are willing to put in the work behind the scenes for months on end to get the chance to do something amazing like that.
I know some of you might not believe it after what I've written about him in recent weeks, but I truly am very happy for Story! He deserves all the credit tonight!
Oh, and in addition to Story's game changing three-run homer, he followed that up by starting double plays on defense to end both the eighth and ninth:
Baseball really is the best!
Studs
Trevor Story: If I didn't put him here, I'd have to legally resign from Over The Monster.
Wilyer Abreu: He looked a little better tonight with a sharp single in the fourth and a walk that turned into a run on Story's three-run shot.
The bullpen: The comeback wouldn't be complete without the pen holding it down, and with Aroldis Chapman unavailable with lat tightness, Wyatt Olds, Alec Gamboa, and Garrett Whitlock combined to go 2.2 scoreless innings.
Duds
Only one dud tonight, and that's me given my recent stance on Story's playing time. The crow is delicious, and I hope it remains on the menu well into October!
One other important note
Just before Story's home run, Willson Contreras was hit in the hand by a pitch and had to leave the game. The good news is x-rays were negative, but given x-rays were also negative after Curtis Mead got hit in July, I'm not going to be celebrating this one until we get further confirmation.

On the other hand, the Nationals will soon get a look at their return from the trade, Connelly Early. The young lefty was on the injured list with elbow inflammation when the Nats traded for him on July 26. He's recently taken some major steps in his rehab.
Washington on September 13 sent Early on a rehab assignment. In one inning with the Triple-A Rochester Red Wings, he allowed three runs on two hits and two walks with two strikeouts.
Nationals President of Baseball Operations (and former Red Sox Assistant General Manager) Paul Toboni confirmed on "The Sports Junkies" show on 106.7 The Fan that Early will make another rehab appearance on September 20 before he makes his DC debut on September 26 against the New York Mets. The season ends on September 28, so Washington will get a look at Early in the major leagues just in time.
Nationals confirm former Red Sox pitcher Connelly Early will make first big league start since trade on September 26
The Nationals were eliminated from playoff contention over the weekend, which could be one reason they're letting Early start. It's already been over two months since the rookie last pitched, but there's no stakes on getting a preview of Early's talent.
Early posted a 3.44 ERA, 1.25 WHIP, 93 strikeouts and 34 walks over 91.2 innings with the Red Sox this season. Washington's rotation hasn't looked sharp lately, despite Cade Cavalli's utter dominance since he faced the Red Sox on June 30 (2.27 ERA, 0.90 WHIP, 112 strikeouts over his last 15 games). Early will be an upgrade over Jake Irvin (5.51 ERA in 96.1 innings) or rookie Jackson Kent (6.40 ERA in 32.1 innings), who has only pitched a tiny sample size of innings, but they haven't been good.
The Red Sox's rotation could use another arm given Patrick Sandoval and Jake Bennett's recent struggles, but holding onto Early wouldn't have done much for them given his long IL stint during the playoff race. Boston dealt from a position of depth to acquire Mead and it deserves credit for doing so despite the unfortunate circumstances that led to his placement on the IL.
Just in the nick of time, the Nationals will get to see what Early can do on the mound before the season ends. The Red Sox may not get so lucky with Mead, even though their season will continue into October.

Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive.
Garrett Crochet has been throwing, Tanner Houck has been on a rehab assignment and even Curtis Mead has been playing catch, among others. While this is the case, the Red Sox gave a negative update on Wednesday. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that reliever Justin Slaten is dealing with "degenerative changes in the flexor mass" and is likely done for the 2026 season.
"Slaten, we got ... he went and saw [Dr. Keith Meister] with our medical staff today and there's some degenerative changes in the flexor mass," Tracy said. "So he's going to be down. He's going to get a PRP injection and it's likely going to end his season. So, that's substantially different news, as far as these guys."
Bad News For Boston
This is a brutal blow for Slaten, and the Red Sox's bullpen in general. Slaten is one of the club's key high-leverage guys, but Boston hasn't had him on the mound since Aug. 12. He was initially placed on the Injured List due to right elbow inflammation. He actually started throwing, but he had to be shut down when the same "symptoms" that landed him on the Injured List popped up again.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 36 appearances, but this doesn't tell the full story about why he's a big loss for Boston. In his final 17 appearances of the season, he had a 2.45 ERA and a 19-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 14 2/3 innings pitched. The first half of the season wasn't great for him, but he had turned things around and looked like the guy Boston hoped it would have out of the bullpen.
The Red Sox have just 11 games left in the 2026 regular season. Losing Slaten hurts Boston's playoff chances. On the bright side, the Red Sox's bullpen could still get better with Houck on a minor league rehab assignment and Garrett Crochet throwing as well. With Slaten likely out for the season, that's one less change Boston will have to make when building the playoff roster. Tyron Guerrero, Crochet, and Houck are all inching their way back. Boston will have to clear three spots to get these guys on the roster. That could be bad news for guys like Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Raymond Burgos, among others.
With Slaten likely not coming back, it's one less decision for Boston to make. Of course, it would be better if he were returning, but that isn't the case right now. Unfortunately, Red Sox fans have seemingly seen the last of Slaten for the 2026 season.

item.content:encoded:
ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.
